To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the extent of 123I-MIBG-derived efferent cardiac sympathetic denervation is related to reduced HRV in the early post-myocardial-infarction period, and that the extent of this denervation is related with the extent of myocardial damage.

decreased heart rate variability, measured 2 weeks after an uncomplicated acute myocardium infarction, was related to the extent, as assessed with 123I-metaiodobenzlyguanidine scinigraphy, of efferent sympathetic denervation of the myocardium.

decreased heart rate variability, measured 2 weeks after an uncomplicated acute myocardian infarction, correlates with the extent of cardiac denervation, as determined by 123-I metaiodobenzlguanidine scinigraphy.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of the relationship between the extent of 123I-metaiodobenzlyguanidine (MIBG) derived efferent sympathetic denervation, assessed by cardiac scintigraphy 2 weeks after acute uncomplicated myocardial infarct, and the extent of heart rate variability (HRV), assessed 2 weeks later, by 24-hr ECG Holter monitoring.
the development of an efficient and accurate algorithm for the analysis of heart rate variability (HRV) signals.
the development of a new type of high performance, high resolution, high sensitivity, and high speed imaging device for the measurement of heart rate variability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
decreased postinfarction HVR is related to the severity of the infarction and the extent of sympathetic denervation.

the decrease in post-myocardial-infarction heart rate variability is due to the decrease of the cardiac efferent sympathetic innervation, which is assessed by metaiodo-benzylguanidin scintigraphy, and is related to the size of the infarcted area.

decreased heart rate variability, as assessed 2 weeks following uncomplicated acute myocardium infarction, reflects cardiac sympathetic denervation, which could be a substrate of reduced post-infarction heart rate variability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the postinfarction denervated heart is a substrate for reduced postinfarct heart rate variability, which in turn is a predictor of sudden death.

the postinfarction reduction in heart rate variability, which has been shown to be a strong prognostic indicator of mortality after myocardial infarctions, is due to the postinfarct sympathetic denervation of the heart.
the extent of 123I-MIBG cardiac denervation is associated with the extent of heart rate variability reduction after uncomplicated acute MI.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have identified a potential mechanism for the increased risk of sudden cardiac death in patients who have had a heart attack.
heart rate variability is a good indicator of cardiac innervation.
we have shown for the first time that there is a strong relationship between the extent of cardiac sympathetic denervation and the degree of heart rate variability.
